by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap. Section 33-1123 is limited to household furniture, furnishings, household goods, consumer electronic devices, and appliances; do not use it for wearing apparel, jewelry, or musical instruments.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate every applicable specific paragraph, then independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), which can protect any property. A dollar ceiling limits protection rather than eligibility. Thus a vehicle remains eligible under § 522(d)(2) above its cap, jewelry uses § 522(d)(4), and § 522(d)(5) remains an additional alternative even when a specific paragraph applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for an unlisted category such as a firearm or jewelry, do not omit a specific paragraph because value exceeds its ceiling, and do not repeat a citation.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is allowable and an eligible asset-exemption pair needs a claim value.
by_task.procedure: Calculate every alternative independently. Use the lesser of asset value and $4,450 under § 522(d)(2), $700 per item under § 522(d)(3), or $1,875 under § 522(d)(4); for jointly owned jewelry of two debtors, § 522(m) makes the § 522(d)(4) ceiling $3,750. Then always value the separate § 522(d)(5) alternative: use the lesser of asset value and $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Because alternatives are evaluated independently, the full unused § 522(d)(1) amount is available; do not reduce § 522(d)(5) merely because no residence claim is listed.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because a specific paragraph applies or the asset is not a residence, and do not use only its $1,475 base amount. Do not exceed $700 per item under § 522(d)(3) or treat that paragraph as covering firearms, jewelry, or other unlisted categories.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the property is held for personal rather than business use.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently as the any-other-property alternative, including when apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid also has a specific exemption. Section (a) covers necessary wearing apparel, (c) covers a motor vehicle, and (e) covers professionally prescribed health aids. A value above a limit does not eliminate either applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 12-1001(d) for ordinary household property; it requires implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry or a watch as necessary wearing apparel under subsection (a), and do not omit subsection (b) merely because a specific subsection applies. Subsection (b) is a personal-property exemption; do not apply it to any real-property interest.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the debtor owns personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Determine eligibility before calculating amounts. Independently include § 12-1001(b) for any debtor-owned personal-use property, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e); a value above its ceiling does not defeat eligibility. Use the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. For a motor vehicle, also report subsection (c) at the lesser of value and $2,400, without doubling that limit. Sections (a) and (e) use the asset value because the supplied text states no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use subsection (d) merely because an item could be called a tool or implement; require facts showing use in the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel, omit subsection (b) because a specific subsection applies, treat either ceiling as an eligibility test, or apply these exemptions to business-use property.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: After checking every specific Oregon category, make a separate § 18.345(1)(p) check for each item of personal property and include it even when a specific exemption also applies, including for a vehicle, firearm, prescribed health aid, or household good.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute subsection (p) for the specific category, apply it to real property, classify wearing apparel as household goods under § 18.345(1)(f), or use vehicle subsection (d) for nonvehicles.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and § 18.345(1)(p) applies to personal property.
by_task.procedure: Report the § 18.345(1)(p) alternative independently at the lesser of the asset value and $400, including when a vehicle, firearm, health aid, or household good also has a specific Oregon exemption. Retain and value the correct specific alternative separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit subsection (p) because the asset exceeds $400 or another subsection applies. Do not classify apparel under subsection (f), use vehicle subsection (d) for household electronics, or replace a specific category with subsection (p).

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and an occupied homestead is jointly owned by two household debtors.
by_task.procedure: Under Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.395(1), report the homestead alternative at the lesser of its value and the $50,000 combined limit. Use the $40,000 limit when only one debtor's homestead interest is involved.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $40,000 single-debtor limit for a jointly owned homestead of two household debtors, and do not apply either homestead limit to personal property.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the debtor owns the property.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the property, whether or not a specific federal or Pennsylvania exemption also applies and whether or not the property's value exceeds the monetary limit.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category, use a specific category belonging to a different kind of property, or treat a firearm as wearing apparel under § 8124(a)(1).

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and § 8123 is evaluated.
by_task.procedure: Report § 8123 independently for every debtor-owned asset. Use the asset value when it is below the applicable ceiling; otherwise use $300 for one debtor or $600 for jointly owned property of two married debtors. Keep this alternative even when a federal or specific Pennsylvania exemption also applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not report the ceiling when the asset value is lower, omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, or use § 8124(a)(3) unless the property is a qualifying sewing machine.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the debtor owns personal property, including property expressly identified as a tool of the debtor's trade.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently for every item of personal property, including when subsection (a), (c), (d), or (e) also applies. Section (a) covers necessary wearing apparel, (c) covers a motor vehicle, (d) covers an implement, professional book, or tool expressly used in the debtor's trade, and (e) covers a professionally prescribed health aid. A value above a limit does not eliminate an applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property. Do not classify jewelry or a watch as necessary wearing apparel, or a device that displays pictures as a family picture. Require express trade-use facts for subsection (d), and do not classify business machinery as a motor vehicle merely because it can move.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the debtor owns personal property or an occupied homestead.
by_task.procedure: Determine eligibility before amounts. For every item of personal property, report § 12-1001(b) independently at the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors, including an expressly identified trade tool and property also covered by (a), (c), (d), or (e). Report subsection (c) for a motor vehicle at the lesser of value and $2,400 without doubling. Report subsection (d) for an expressly identified trade tool at the lesser of value and $1,500 for one debtor or $3,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Subsections (a) and (e) use asset value. For an equal-half jointly owned occupied homestead, § 12-901 gives a $15,000 proportionate-share claim, not one combined $30,000 claim.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply personal-property subsections to real property, including burial realty or a homestead. Do not use subsection (d) without express trade-use facts, subsection (c) for business machinery that is not a motor vehicle, or subsection (a) for jewelry, a watch, or a device merely capable of displaying family pictures. Do not treat any dollar ceiling as an eligibility test.

operations.rationale: The parent repeatedly omitted § 12-1001(b) from above-cap vehicles and expressly identified trade tools, omitted subsection (d) because trade-property value exceeded its limit, and misclassified trade machinery under subsection (c). It also applied the personal-property wildcard to real property and doubled the joint homestead amount. These sources support separate corrections for missing overlapping alternatives, category boundaries, and claim amounts while preserving the express-facts requirement for trade tools.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: After checking every specific Oregon category, make a separate § 18.345(1)(p) check for each item of personal property and include it even when a specific exemption also applies, including for a vehicle, firearm, prescribed health aid, or household good.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute subsection (p) for the specific category, apply it to real property, classify wearing apparel as household goods under § 18.345(1)(f), or use vehicle subsection (d) for nonvehicles.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and § 18.345(1)(p) applies to personal property.
by_task.procedure: Report the § 18.345(1)(p) alternative independently at the lesser of the asset value and $400, including when a vehicle, firearm, health aid, or household good also has a specific Oregon exemption. Retain and value the correct specific alternative separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit subsection (p) because the asset exceeds $400 or another subsection applies. Do not classify apparel under subsection (f), use vehicle subsection (d) for household electronics, or replace a specific category with subsection (p).

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and an occupied homestead is jointly owned by two household debtors.
by_task.procedure: Under Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.395(1), report the homestead alternative at the lesser of its value and the $50,000 combined limit. Use the $40,000 limit when only one debtor's homestead interest is involved.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $40,000 single-debtor limit for a jointly owned homestead of two household debtors, and do not apply either homestead limit to personal property.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the debtor owns the property.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the property, whether or not a specific federal or Pennsylvania exemption also applies and whether or not the property's value exceeds the monetary limit.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category, use a specific category belonging to a different kind of property, or treat a firearm as wearing apparel under § 8124(a)(1).

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and § 8123 is evaluated.
by_task.procedure: Report § 8123 independently for every debtor-owned asset. Use the asset value when it is below the applicable ceiling; otherwise use $300 for one debtor or $600 for jointly owned property of two married debtors. Keep this alternative even when a federal or specific Pennsylvania exemption also applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not report the ceiling when the asset value is lower, omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, or use § 8124(a)(3) unless the property is a qualifying sewing machine.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the property is held for personal rather than business use.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently as the any-other-property alternative, including when apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid also has a specific exemption. Section (a) covers necessary wearing apparel, (c) covers a motor vehicle, and (e) covers professionally prescribed health aids. A value above a limit does not eliminate either applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 12-1001(d) for ordinary household property; it requires implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry or a watch as necessary wearing apparel under subsection (a), and do not omit subsection (b) merely because a specific subsection applies. Subsection (b) is a personal-property exemption; do not apply it to any real-property interest.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the debtor owns personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Determine eligibility before calculating amounts. Independently include § 12-1001(b) for any debtor-owned personal-use property, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e); a value above its ceiling does not defeat eligibility. Use the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. For a motor vehicle, also report subsection (c) at the lesser of value and $2,400, without doubling that limit. Sections (a) and (e) use the asset value because the supplied text states no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use subsection (d) merely because an item could be called a tool or implement; require facts showing use in the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel, omit subsection (b) because a specific subsection applies, treat either ceiling as an eligibility test, or apply these exemptions to business-use property. Subsection (b) applies only to personal property, not to any real-property interest.

operations.rationale: In source 281, the parent correctly used § 12-1001(b) for the debtor's personal property but also extended it to a real-property interest. The supplied statute confines § 12-1001 to personal property. This narrow boundary correction removes that false positive while preserving the existing overlap, category, cap, and trade-use instructions verbatim.

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap. Section 33-1123 is limited to household furniture, furnishings, household goods, consumer electronic devices, and appliances; do not use it for wearing apparel, jewelry, or musical instruments.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate every applicable specific paragraph, then independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), which can protect any property. A dollar ceiling limits protection rather than eligibility. Thus a vehicle remains eligible under § 522(d)(2) above its cap, jewelry uses § 522(d)(4), and § 522(d)(5) remains an additional alternative even when a specific paragraph applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for an unlisted category such as a firearm or jewelry, do not omit a specific paragraph because value exceeds its ceiling, and do not repeat a citation.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is allowable and an eligible asset-exemption pair needs a claim value.
by_task.procedure: Calculate every alternative independently. Use the lesser of asset value and $4,450 under § 522(d)(2), $700 per item under § 522(d)(3), or $1,875 under § 522(d)(4); for jointly owned jewelry of two debtors, § 522(m) makes the § 522(d)(4) ceiling $3,750. Then always value the separate § 522(d)(5) alternative: use the lesser of asset value and $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Because alternatives are evaluated independently, the full unused § 522(d)(1) amount is available; do not reduce § 522(d)(5) merely because no residence claim is listed.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because a specific paragraph applies or the asset is not a residence, and do not use only its $1,475 base amount. Do not exceed $700 per item under § 522(d)(3) or treat that paragraph as covering firearms, jewelry, or other unlisted categories.
